In 2025, **4,514 NYC crashes injured or killed at least one cyclist**. Those crashes hurt 4,584 cyclists in total, because some crashes hurt more than one.

Things to know before relying on this number:
- **What it counts:** This is the number of crashes, not the number of cyclists. A crash is included if NYPD recorded at least one cyclist injured or killed in it. The data covers the whole year, from January 1 to December 31, 2025.
- **Where the data comes from:** These are NYPD crash reports. A crash with a hurt cyclist that police never reported isn't included, so the true number is probably higher.
- **Comparing with Boston:** Boston's crash data is based on ambulance calls rather than police reports, so the two cities' numbers can't be compared directly.

ANSWER: 4514

NYPD crash reports show **22 cyclists killed in NYC in 2024**. There were 91,316 crashes that year, all with distinct IDs and no missing cyclist-death counts. Each of 22 separate crashes killed one cyclist.

Before relying on this number:
- **These are police reports.** The table counts deaths as the police recorded them on each collision report. Later reclassifications or deaths that happened well after the crash may not show up here.
- **Other official counts may be higher.** NYC DOT's Vision Zero figures sometimes differ from the NYPD numbers. One likely reason is how riders of e-bikes, mopeds and scooters are categorised: some are recorded as "motorists" rather than "cyclists". Treat 22 as the count of people NYPD reports labelled as cyclists, not necessarily every bike-related death.

ANSWER: 22

NYPD crash reports show **4,114 cyclists injured** in NYC so far in 2026.

Before relying on this number:
- **It covers part of the year.** The data runs from January 1 to November 3, 2026, so this is a year-to-date figure, not a full-year total. NYPD reports can also come in late, so the last few days may not be complete yet.
- **It doesn't include deaths.** Another 5 cyclists were killed. Counting injuries and deaths together gives 4,119 cyclists hurt.
- **It only includes crashes police reported.** Cyclist injuries with no NYPD report aren't counted, so the true number is probably higher.
- **The months vary a lot.** Injuries ran about 130–160 a month in January and February, and about 520–570 a month from May through October.

ANSWER: 4114

Manhattan had the most crashes that hurt a cyclist in 2025, with **1,542**. I counted NYPD-reported collisions from January 1 to December 31, 2025 where at least one cyclist was injured or killed.

| Borough | Crashes that hurt a cyclist | Cyclists hurt |
|---|---|---|
| Manhattan | 1,542 | 1,570 |
| Brooklyn | 1,452 | 1,471 |
| Queens | 883 | 898 |
| Bronx | 461 | 467 |
| No borough recorded | 124 | 125 |
| Staten Island | 52 | 53 |

Things to know before relying on this:
- **The count is crashes, not people.** Some crashes hurt more than one cyclist, so Manhattan had 1,570 cyclists hurt across those 1,542 crashes.
- **Some crashes have no borough.** NYPD didn't record a borough for 124 of these crashes. Manhattan leads Brooklyn by only 90, so if most of those 124 happened in Brooklyn, the ranking could change. Whichever way they fall, the two boroughs are close.
- **Only police-reported crashes are included.** Cyclist injuries that were never reported to NYPD aren't in this data.
- **These are raw counts.** They don't adjust for how much cycling happens in each borough.

ANSWER: 1542

NYPD crash reports list **107 pedestrians killed** in NYC in 2023. They come from 106 separate crashes, out of 96,608 crashes reported that year. Every 2023 record has a value in the pedestrian-deaths field, and no crash appears twice.

Some things to know before you rely on this number:
- **These are police crash reports.** The count only includes deaths NYPD recorded in its crash data. If a pedestrian died days later and the report wasn't updated, they may not be counted. Official figures, such as NYC DOT's Vision Zero totals, are compiled differently and can be somewhat different.
- **The count covers the whole city.** I didn't filter by borough, so the roughly 29% of crashes with no borough recorded are included.
- **Boston's crash data isn't comparable.** It's based on ambulance calls rather than police reports, so it can't be compared one-to-one with this number.

ANSWER: 107

7,100 of the 85,559 NYC crashes reported by police in 2025 have no borough recorded. That's about 8.3%.

- **Blank borough isn't the same as unknown location.** 6,815 of those 7,100 crashes still have latitude and longitude, so most of them could be placed in a borough from their coordinates. Only 285 have neither a borough nor a location.
- **2025 is much better than the dataset overall.** The table notes say about 29% of all crashes have no borough. Be careful comparing borough totals across years, because the share of missing boroughs changes a lot.
- **There are no hidden blanks.** The borough field holds only the five borough names or nothing; there are no empty strings or "Unknown" values.
- **The year looks complete.** The data runs through 2025-12-31. The count covers only crashes the NYPD filed a report for.

ANSWER: 7100

The summer 2025 average at Washington Street north of Bexley Road (location 60) was **546.5 bikes per day**.

That figure comes from just two days of counting:
- Wednesday, June 11, 2025: 552 bikes (82°F, fair)
- Thursday, June 12, 2025: 541 bikes (86°F, fair)

Each count covers 24 hours and both directions. I checked the hourly data and both days have all 24 hours, adding up to the same totals.

Before relying on this number:
- **It isn't a season-long average.** Boston counts each location for about two days at a time, a few times a year. "Summer" here means one mid-June count on two warm, dry weekdays. Weekends and July–August aren't included.
- **It's higher than earlier years.** Earlier June counts at this spot averaged about 470 in 2024 and about 330 in 2023. Two days of data per year can't separate a real trend from weather or day-to-day noise.

ANSWER: 546.5

The average was about **652 bikes per count day** in summer 2024, across all Boston count locations.

That figure is the plain mean of 160 location-days of counts from 83 locations. Each day is a 24-hour count in both directions. Most of the counts were taken June 11–12 (121 of the 160 location-days). The rest were spread from late June to July 10.

Before relying on the number:
- **It's not an every-day average.** Each location is counted for only about two days at a time, so this is a snapshot of those days, not a full-season average.
- **A few busy spots raise the average.** Daily counts ranged from 5 to 4,364 bikes. A typical location probably sees fewer than 652, and five counts on June 18 averaged about 1,500.
- **Comparisons are uneven.** Different seasons count different sets of locations. For example, only 35–36 locations were counted in the 2024 winter and spring rounds, against 83 in summer. Compare against the same season in other years rather than across seasons.

ANSWER: 652.41

About 0.045 (4.5%) of all counted traffic in Boston's 2025 counts was bikes.

**How I got it:** I added up every 2025 count day: 438 location-days at 91 locations, from March 11 to December 10, 2025.
- Bikes: 303,464
- Motor vehicles: 6,510,976
- Bike fraction: 303,464 ÷ 6,814,440 = 0.0445

**Before relying on this number:**
- **Pooled versus averaged:** 0.0445 is the share of all traffic added together. If you instead average the share at each location-day, you get about 0.093. That's higher because quiet, bike-heavy spots count as much as busy roads.
- **Days with no vehicles counted:** 19 location-days recorded zero vehicles. Two of the locations are off-street paths (Southwest Corridor and Neponset Greenway), so zero is real there. The third, Atlantic Avenue south of Commercial Street, is a street, so its 8 zero-vehicle days probably mean the counter only covered the bike lane. Dropping all 19 days lowers the share to about 0.042.
- **Not a citywide measure:** Each location is only counted for about two days at a time, a few times a year, and the sites aren't chosen at random. This is the bike share of the traffic that was counted, not of all Boston traffic.

ANSWER: 0.0445

The data shows **48 different Boston bike count locations** counted in 2026. That comes from 136 location-days between March 10 and September 17, 2026.

2026 is probably not a complete year. In recent years, counting has run into December. 2025 covered 91 locations and 2024 covered 89. The 2026 data stops in mid-September, so autumn counts are likely still missing and this number will probably go up. Don't compare it with full-year totals from earlier years.

ANSWER: 48

The busiest Boston count location in 2025 was **Massachusetts Avenue north of Back Street** (location 44), with an average of **4,588.75 bikes per count day**. The next highest was the BU Bridge north of Commonwealth Avenue at about 2,185, so Mass Ave averaged roughly twice as many.

Things to know before relying on this number:
- **The average covers only 8 days.** Boston doesn't count bikes every day. Each location gets an automated 24-hour count, both directions, for about two days at a time a few times a year. In 2025 this location was counted twice in each season: March, June, September and December.
- **Winter brings the average down.** Daily counts ran from 2,900 to 2,924 in December and from 5,904 to 6,045 in September.
- **Locations weren't counted the same way, so comparing their averages isn't quite fair.** Several were counted only in the fall, which tends to give higher averages. Mass Ave still wins clearly: its two fall days alone (about 5,975) beat every other location's average.
- None of the 2025 count days at this location had missing bike counts.

ANSWER: 4588.75

Across all of Boston's hourly bike counts, **5 PM (hour 17)** has the most bikes: 234,843 in total. The morning commute peak at 8 AM is second with 208,826, followed by 6 PM with 178,884. Overall the counts show a typical two-peak commuter pattern.

Things to know before relying on this:
- **The comparison is fair across hours.** Every hour has almost the same number of records (5,738 each, except 5,735 for midnight) across the same 147 count days. So the ranking isn't caused by some hours being counted more often.
- **These aren't continuous counts.** Boston counts each location for about two days at a time, a few times a year. The totals describe those sampled days at the counted locations, not every bike trip in the city.
- **Hours are local time.** The source stores times in UTC and the table converts them to Boston time.

ANSWER: 17

Boston's Vision Zero data recorded **366 crashes involving a person on a bike in 2024**. That's the count of records with mode = "bike" between January 1 and December 31, 2024, and none of the records are duplicates.

Before relying on this number:
- **It only covers crashes where someone called an ambulance.** Each record is an EMS dispatch, so bike crashes with no ambulance call aren't counted. The real number of bike crashes is higher.
- **Each crash has one mode.** If a crash involved both a bike and a pedestrian, it may be counted under only one of them.
- **You can't compare it directly with NYC.** NYC's crash data comes from police reports, which are collected differently.
- **For context,** the same data shows 465 pedestrian crashes and 2,627 motor-vehicle-only crashes in Boston in 2024.

ANSWER: 366

I counted 555,121 Bluebikes trips in September 2026.

- **How I counted:** I added up the daily trip counts for September 1–30, 2026. All 30 days are in the data, so the month is complete.
- **What's included:** Every member type and bike type is counted. That includes e-bike trips that didn't start at a station.
- **Dates:** Trips are assigned to the day they started, using local Boston time.
- **Data range:** The table only goes from October 31, 2025 to October 31, 2026. That means you can't compare this to Septembers in earlier years with this data.

ANSWER: 555121

About 0.40 of Bluebikes trips in October 2026 were on electric bikes: 230,879 of 571,583 trips. The other 340,704 were on classic bikes.

Things to know before relying on this number:
- **Data coverage:** October has data for all 31 days, and the bikes are recorded as only two types, classic or electric. All October trips have a start station. No e-bike trips that started away from a station show up in this table for these months.
- **August jump:** The e-bike share rose sharply in August 2026. It was about 0.26 in June and July, then about 0.37 in August and September, and 0.40 in October. In that time e-bike trips went up by about 73,000 a month while classic trips fell only slightly. That could be a real change, such as more e-bikes in the fleet, or a change in how trips are recorded. Either way, October's share shouldn't be treated as typical of earlier months.
- **Unit of count:** These are counts of trips, not riders or distance.

ANSWER: 0.404

Casual Bluebikes riders averaged about **25.3 minutes per trip** in July 2026.

That figure comes from 184,770 casual trips across all 31 days of the month, totalling about 4.67 million minutes. Every trip had a usable duration, so none were left out. I divided total minutes by total trips, which gives each trip equal weight.

Before relying on the number:
- **A few very long trips raise the average.** Some station-day groups average close to 25 hours per trip, which probably means bikes that weren't docked or returned late. A typical casual trip is closer to 17 minutes, but that's a rough figure: it's the median of the per-group averages, not of individual trips.
- **Bike type makes a difference.** Classic-bike casual trips averaged about 26.9 minutes and e-bike trips about 19.6 minutes.
- **For comparison,** across June to October 2026, casual riders averaged about 23.5 minutes and members about 13.3 minutes.

ANSWER: 25.26

687 NYC street segments got their first protected bike lane in 2023, with install dates from January 18 to December 30, 2023. Each segment is counted once, so a lane added to a segment that already had one isn't included.

Before relying on this number:
- **Segments, not miles:** this counts pieces of street, and they vary in length, so it doesn't tell you how much lane was built.
- **Two are gone:** 2 of the 687 segments no longer have a current bike facility record. If you only want lanes still in place, the count is 685.
- **The dates have problems:** some segments have first-install years as early as 1894. Those are almost certainly placeholder or bad dates, not real installs. The table also includes 2026 dates. The 2023 group's dates look reasonable, but install dates in this table aren't fully reliable.
- **2023 is the highest year in the table:** it's above 2022 (438) and 2024 (566).

ANSWER: 687

The number of cyclists hurt near these lanes went up by about 17% (0.173) after installation, not down.

**What I measured:** I used 4,349 protected bike lane segments in NYC that were installed between 1 Jan 2015 and 24 Oct 2024. For each one, I counted cyclists injured or killed in crashes within about 50 m, in the two years before installation and the two years after.
- Before: 4,207 cyclists hurt
- After: 4,935 cyclists hurt
- Change: (4,935 − 4,207) / 4,207 ≈ 0.173

**Things to know before relying on this number:**
- **Some crashes are counted more than once.** A crash near where two segments meet is counted once for each segment. So these totals are bigger than the real number of distinct people hurt.
- **This doesn't show the lanes made streets more dangerous.** Over the same windows, cyclist injuries across the whole city rose only about 1.7%. So the rise near new lanes was larger than the city trend. But lanes usually go where many people already ride, and riding often increases once a lane opens. Without data on how many people rode there, we can't tell whether each ride got safer or riskier.
- **The results vary a lot by year.** For example, lanes installed in 2020 went from 685 to 1,023 people hurt, which overlaps with the cycling boom during COVID. Lanes installed in 2019 and 2022 saw small drops.
- **The after windows are complete.** Crash data runs to November 2026, so even the lanes installed in late 2024 have a full two years of after data.
- **Some crashes are missing.** About 11% of NYPD crash reports have no location, so those can't be matched to any lane. Both counts are somewhat low because of this.

ANSWER: 0.173

In Brooklyn, the number of cyclists hurt near new protected lanes went up by about 0.435 (43.5%) when comparing the two years before installation with the two years after.

- **What's counted:** 843 Brooklyn protected-lane segments installed between January 1, 2015 and September 30, 2024.
- **Cyclists hurt within about 50 m:** 931 in the two years before installation and 1,336 in the two years after.
- **Change:** (1,336 − 931) / 931 = **0.435**.

Things to know before relying on this number:
- **One crash can count more than once.** A crash near several neighbouring segments is counted once for each segment, so the totals overstate the number of distinct people hurt. The fractional change is less affected, but it is still weighted towards places where segments cluster together.
- **It's not a measure of risk.** There's no data on how many people ride. New protected lanes usually bring more cyclists, so more injuries nearby doesn't necessarily mean each trip got more dangerous.
- **The citywide trend doesn't explain it.** Over the same two-year windows, citywide cyclist injuries rose only about 0.014, so the jump near the new lanes is much bigger than the background trend.
- **Possible data glitch:** the latest crash date in the dataset is November 3, 2026, which looks wrong. It doesn't change this result: every Brooklyn segment was installed early enough for its full two years after installation to fall within the data.
- **NYPD crash reports are incomplete.** About 11% have no location, so they can't be matched to any segment.

ANSWER: 0.435

Across the same before and after windows, cyclists hurt citywide in NYC went up by about 1.7% (0.0175).

**How I got this:** the lane safety table has 4,349 protected-lane segments installed from 1 January 2015 to 24 October 2024. For each segment, it counts cyclists hurt (injured plus killed) across the whole city in the two years before and the two years after that segment's install date. I added up those citywide counts over all segments and compared the totals:
- Before: 42,938,858
- After: 43,689,583
- Change: 43,689,583 ÷ 42,938,858 − 1 = 0.0175

**Things to know before relying on this number:**
- **It's weighted by segments.** Each segment adds its own citywide window to the total, so the same crashes are counted many times. The totals are not real counts of people. The result is a weighted average of the citywide trend, and years with many installs count for more.
- **Compare it with the lane-level figure.** Within about 50 m of the new lanes, cyclists hurt rose 17% (4,207 to 4,935). That's well above the 1.7% citywide rise, but it isn't adjusted for more people riding on the new lanes. Also, a crash near two adjacent segments is counted once for each segment.
- **Data caveats:** the crash data is NYPD reports, so it only includes crashes police recorded. The latest crash date in the data is 3 November 2026, so the after windows for the latest installs look fully covered, but that date is worth checking.

ANSWER: 0.0175

In 2025, **4,514** police-reported crashes in New York City injured or killed at least one cyclist.

The data includes all 12 months of 2025, from 204 crashes in February to 539 in August. The metric's warning that the current year is incomplete applies to 2026, which has data only into early November.

Before relying on this number, keep in mind:
- **It counts crashes, not people.** One crash that hurt two cyclists counts once. The number of cyclists hurt is a separate metric.
- **Only crashes the NYPD reported are included.** Crashes that were never reported are missing. Don't compare this directly with Boston's crash counts, which come from ambulance dispatches.
- **It doesn't account for how many people ride.** Cycling in NYC has grown, so changes from year to year don't directly show whether riding got safer. For reference, there were 5,084 such crashes in 2024 and 5,125 in 2023.

ANSWER: 4514

NYPD crash reports list **22 cyclists killed in NYC in 2024**.

Things to know before relying on this number:
- **It only counts police reports.** It is the total of deaths recorded in the NYPD crash data. A person who dies some time after the crash may not be added to the original report, so official city traffic-death totals can be higher.
- **2024 is a full year in this data.** The "current year is partial" warning applies to 2026, not 2024.
- **Earlier years for context:** 19 in 2022, 31 in 2023 and 22 in 2024. These counts don't account for how many people ride, which has grown.

ANSWER: 22

NYPD-reported crashes injured **4,114 cyclists** in NYC in 2026 so far. I got this from the `nyc_cyclists_injured` metric.

Things to know before you rely on this number:
- **The year isn't over.** The data runs from January 1 to November 3, 2026, and November only has its first three days. So this isn't a full-year total. Even so, it's already close to the 4,574 for all of 2025.
- **Recent days may still change.** The last few days are likely to grow as more reports come in.
- **Only police reports are counted.** Injuries that weren't in an NYPD crash report are missing.
- **The count doesn't adjust for how many people ride.** Ridership has grown, so a higher count doesn't necessarily mean riding got more dangerous.
- **This counts people, not crashes.** One crash can injure more than one cyclist.

ANSWER: 4114

According to NYPD crash reports, **107 pedestrians were killed in NYC crashes in 2023**.

In summer 2025, an average of **546.5 bikes per day** were counted on Washington Street north of Bexley Road.

That figure comes from only **2 count days**: June 11 (552 bikes) and June 12 (541 bikes), 2025. Both days were fair and warm, with highs of 82° and 86°. Each day's count covers 24 hours in both directions.

Before relying on it:
- **It's a very small sample.** The city counts each location for about two days a few times a year, so a single weekday or a change in weather can move the average a lot. Treat it as a snapshot, not a summer-long average.
- **Compare it only with other summers.** The city has also counted in winter and spring since 2020, and those counts are lower. Earlier summer counts here averaged 467.5 in 2024, 327.5 in 2023 and 388 in 2022, so 2025 is the highest summer on record at this spot until 2026. Even so, the two-day samples mean that rise is suggestive rather than conclusive.

ANSWER: 546.5

In summer 2024, Boston's bike count locations averaged **about 652 bikes per count day**.

That comes from 104,386 bikes counted over 160 location-days. Dividing those gives the same figure as the metric, so no days were left out of the average.

Before relying on this number:
- **The sample is small.** Each location is counted for only about two days, a few times a year, so averages like this can swing a lot.
- **Compare summer with summer.** Since 2020 the City also counts in winter and spring, which pulls down averages that mix seasons. Summer 2024 should only be compared with other summers.
- **It's a count-day average.** It's the mean of the location-days that were counted, not a measured daily average for each site or for the city as a whole.

ANSWER: 652.41

In Boston's 2025 counts, bikes were about **0.0445** of all counted traffic: 303,464 bikes out of 6,814,440 bikes plus motor vehicles. That's across 438 location-days counted between March and December 2025.

Things to know before relying on this number:
- **It's a sample, not a year-round total.** Each location is counted for about two days, a few times a year. The figure describes those count days, not all traffic in Boston.
- **Seasons are mixed.** The 2025 counts include winter and spring days, when fewer people ride. Compare it only with other all-season years.
- **Some vehicles are counted twice.** "Meridian Street south of Nay Street" has two location IDs. On 8 days in 2025 they report different bike counts but the same vehicle count, so about 155,000 vehicles appear twice. Counting those vehicles once gives a share of 0.0456. The bike counts differ, so they may be two separate counters. Either way the answer moves by about 0.001.
- **Context:** the share was 0.0438 in 2024 and 0.0436 in 2023, so 2025 is slightly higher.

ANSWER: 0.0445

Boston counted bikes at **48 different locations** in 2026.

- **How I counted:** I listed the 2026 count days for each location and got 48 location names. A direct count of distinct names gave 48 too, and still 48 after ignoring capitalisation and extra spaces. Locations are identified only by name, so two names for the same spot would be counted twice. None of the names look like duplicates.
- **What "counted" means:** each location is counted for about two days at a time, a few times a year. In 2026, most locations had 2 count days, many had 4, and one (Blue Hill Avenue north of Rexford Street) had 6. These are short counting sessions, not continuous counters.
- **Date range:** the 2026 counts in the data run from March 10 to September 17. If the year isn't over or later counts haven't been loaded yet, the final number could be higher.

ANSWER: 48

In 2025, **Massachusetts Avenue north of Back Street** had the highest average: **4,588.75 bikes per count day**. That's more than twice the next location, BU Bridge north of Commonwealth Avenue (2,184.5 over 6 count days). Longfellow Bridge came third at 1,815.25 over 8 days.

The lead is so large that I checked the individual days. The counts are steady across all four counting periods, so one odd day isn't driving the result:
- **Spring (Mar 11–12):** 4,526 and 3,677
- **Summer (Jun 11–12):** 5,679 and 5,055
- **Fall (Sep 16–17):** 5,904 and 6,045
- **Winter (Dec 3–4):** 2,924 and 2,900

Before relying on the number:
- **It's a small sample.** The figure covers 8 count days in total, two in each season. With so few days, averages can move a lot.
- **Some locations have even less data.** Several were counted only twice in 2025 (for example, North Harvard Street at 1,673.5). The ranking compares sites with different amounts of data and different seasons.
- **Winter and spring counts lower the average.** The City now counts in all seasons. This site's summer and fall days alone average about 5,670. To compare across years, use the same season.

ANSWER: 4588.75

The busiest hour is **17 (5–6 pm local time)**, with 234,843 bikes counted. That's 12% more than the morning peak at 8 am (208,826). The next busiest hours are 6 pm (178,884), 4 pm (146,597) and 9 am (136,639). The fewest bikes were counted at 3 am (2,322).

No metric breaks counts down by hour, so I added up bikes by hour in the hourly count table.

Before you rely on this:
- **Coverage is even across hours.** Every hour has 5,738 rows across the same 91 locations, except midnight, which has 5,735. So hours can be compared fairly.
- **It's not a continuous record.** Boston counts each location for about two days at a time, a few times a year. These totals reflect which locations and days were sampled, not the whole city's traffic.
- **The timestamps were converted.** The source stores times in UTC and the table converts them to Boston local time. The afternoon peak is far ahead of the next hour, so a slight conversion error around daylight saving changes wouldn't affect the answer.

ANSWER: 17

Boston's Vision Zero data recorded **366 crashes involving a person on a bike in 2024**.

Before you rely on this number:
- **Only crashes with an ambulance call are counted.** The data comes from EMS dispatches, so bike crashes where no ambulance was called aren't included. The real number of crashes is higher.
- **Don't compare it directly with New York City figures.** NYC's crash counts come from police reports, which is a different way of recording crashes.
- **For context:** 2024 was a bit lower than 2023 (391) and about the same as 2019 (365). The lowest years were 2021–2022, at about 240 each.

In 2023, 687 NYC street segments got their first protected bike lane. That's the most of any year in the data, which covers 2015 through October 2024. The next highest year is 2020, with 512.

Before relying on this number:
- **It counts segments, not distance.** Segments vary in length, so 687 doesn't tell you how many miles of lane were added.
- **Only first protected lanes count.** A segment that already had a protected lane and got an upgrade or replacement in 2023 isn't included.

ANSWER: 687

Within about 50 m of the 4,349 street segments that got their first protected bike lane between 2015 and October 2024, cyclists hurt rose from **4,207** in the two years before installation to **4,935** in the two years after. That's an increase of **0.173** (17.3%) over the before count.

Things to know before relying on this number:
- **The whole city changed too.** Using the same two-year windows around each install, cyclist injuries across NYC rose only about 0.017. So injuries near the new lanes grew about 0.156 more than the city as a whole.
- **More riders isn't accounted for.** Lanes tend to go where riding is already growing, so more riders after a lane opens means more people who can get hurt. There are no ridership counts by street to adjust for this, so the increase doesn't mean the lanes made streets more dangerous.
- **Some injuries are counted more than once.** A crash near several neighbouring segments counts once for each segment, which inflates both the before and after totals.
- **The pandemic skews 2020.** Lanes installed in 2020 have after-windows during the pandemic, and they show the biggest jump: 685 before to 1,023 after.
- **Recent lanes may have short after-windows.** Lanes from 2023–2024 may not have two full years of data after installation yet. The 2024 lanes show 151 before and 156 after. I'm inferring this from the dates; I didn't confirm it in the data.

ANSWER: 0.173

In Brooklyn, the number of cyclists hurt near new protected lanes rose by about 44% (0.435) from the two years before each lane went in to the two years after.

- **Scope:** 843 Brooklyn street segments got their first protected lane between 2015 and October 2024.
- **Counts:** 931 cyclists were hurt within about 50 m of these segments in the two years before installation, and 1,336 in the two years after.
- **Citywide comparison:** Over the same windows, cyclist injuries across NYC barely changed (+0.014). So injuries near Brooklyn's new lanes grew about 0.42 more than the citywide trend. That gap is much larger than in Manhattan (−0.02), Queens (+0.20) or the Bronx (+0.32).

Things to know before relying on this number:
- **Riders:** It doesn't mean the lanes made streets more dangerous. Lanes tend to go where riding is growing, and new lanes attract more riders. There are no per-street ridership counts, so the figure can't be adjusted for that extra exposure.
- **Double counting:** A crash near several adjacent segments counts once for each segment. This inflates the raw before and after totals.
- **Pandemic:** For lanes installed in 2020 or later, the comparison windows include the pandemic, when riding patterns changed.
- **Recent lanes:** For lanes installed late in the period, the two-year "after" window may run past the end of the available crash data. If so, their after counts would be too low.

ANSWER: 0.435
